quote: Spinoza suggested that we first passively accept a proposition in the course of comprehending it, and only afterward actively disbelieve propositions which are rejected by consideration.
content: Gilbert's Spinozan hypothesis, that we automatically accept a proposition just by comprehending it and must spend effort to "unbelieve" it, is elegant but contested. The supporting studies are small and from the early-1990s social-cognition tradition whose paradigms have weathered the replication crisis poorly, and direct challenges exist: Hasson, Simmons & Todorov (2005) found people do not automatically accept implausible statements, with the "belief by default" pattern depending on prior plausibility rather than holding universally. Richter et al. (2009) likewise found readers routinely validate incoming claims against knowledge. The model is influential, not established.

quote: Subjects in the cognitively busy condition recommended an average of 11.15 years in prison
content: The dramatic crime-report result, busy subjects giving nearly double the sentence when false statements aggravated the crime, comes from a single experiment (Gilbert, Tafarodi & Malone 1993) with a modest sample, and I know of no large direct replication. Note also that the effect appears only under deliberate cognitive load, an unusual condition; the non-busy subjects barely differed (7.03 vs 6.03 years). So even on its own terms the study shows that ordinary, undistracted readers largely succeed at rejecting clearly-labeled falsehoods, a much milder conclusion than the paper's title, "You Can't Not Believe Everything You Read."
